Sen. Kirt’s study examines gaps in mental health treatment for legal guardians
Senate Democratic Leader Julia Kirt led an interim study at the Oklahoma Capitol focusing on barriers faced by legal guardians supporting relatives with serious mental illness. Families testified about difficulties communicating with treatment facilities due to privacy laws and procedural delays. The study aims to identify policy gaps while safeguarding patient rights.
Senate Democratic Leader Julia Kirt held an interim study at the Oklahoma state Capitol on Oct. 1 examining challenges faced by families and legal guardians in accessing information and supporting loved ones with serious mental illness. The study focused on the role of legal guardians and caregivers in mental health treatment, highlighting how current Oklahoma policies may hinder families from assisting those unable to make medical decisions themselves.
Testimony was provided by representatives from the National Alliance on Mental Illness Oklahoma, the Oklahoma Department of Mental Health and Substance Abuse Services, and family members serving as legal guardians. Guardianships are approved by courts when individuals cannot make certain medical or financial decisions; however, families reported difficulty getting state agencies and treatment facilities to recognize their authority once appointed.
State officials discussed balancing verification of guardianship with compliance to medical privacy laws. Family members described negative outcomes when communication is delayed or lacking between facilities and those legally responsible for patients' care. “The stories I’ve heard from guardians are stark. Caregivers have described not being able to speak to doctors to provide health history or even know where their loved one is,” said Kirt. “We’ve heard about patients being checked out without the guardian even being told, and loved ones ending up in jail.”
A central issue discussed was how federal privacy protections can delay information sharing even after a court appoints a guardian, sometimes resulting in serious consequences for patients and families. Sarah Smith recounted her experience waiting for facility staff to verify her guardianship as her sister was released without notification; Charla Collins described similar difficulties involving her adult daughter’s repeated discharges without her knowledge.
Kirt said it is critical to improve procedures so that legal guardians can quickly be included in patient care: “When someone is experiencing a serious mental health crisis, their family shouldn’t have to fight the system just to find out where they are or help provide doctors with critical information,” said Kirt. She added that protecting patient rights while ensuring effective support remains a priority.
